utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Good morning to you, Witness. I have to remind you again that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May God's will reign in this house. May there be peace in this house, and I wish that this trial be concluded according to God's wishes and not necessarily mine. Thank you, Mr. Presiding Judge. Last time, we left it off when we discussed a topic concerning the outbreak of hostilities in Zepa and Srebrenica. I will have a few questions of you about the War Presidency, the Executive Board, and the president of the War Presidency, given that it was frequently mentioned here and in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please clarify for the Chamber what the role of the president of the Presidency was. Am I correct if I say that according to the then regulation, it should have been occupied by the municipal president? Given that Zepa had not been a municipality, another solution had to be come up with. Could you please explain who elected presidents of war presidencies and specifically the president in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Good morning to you as well.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is as follows: You are correct when you say that under the then legislation of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, automatically, the municipal president in war conditions also as the president of the War Presidency. You also said that given that Zepa had not enjoyed municipal status, it was only a part of a municipality, I can tell you what I know about how presidents of war presidencies were elected. As far as I know, and from what I could gather later, the first president of the War Presidency, I don't know whether he was appointed by anyone or he was nominated by a group of prominent people in Zepa. They obviously believed that this person would be best suited to fill that position. As of 1993 onwards, presidents of the War Presidency were appointed by Sarajevo. I don't know whether it was the party who did that or some other political body. It is most likely that the party, the SDA, appointed them, because they received the most votes among the Muslim population. This is as far as my knowledge goes about any appointments and removals of presidents of war presidencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who was the first, the second, and the third president?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, and I said that in my previous testimony on Thursday, I believe, the first War Presidency president was Mr. Benjamin Kulovac. The second, Ago Padzic, and the third, Mehmed Hajric. If there were any other people in between, I can't recall them. This is what I can remember, more or less.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir. Could the witness and the accused be reminded to pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We didn't receive interpretation of the last portion of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Nor was the question heard, Your Honour, because the microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether all three presidents of the War Presidency were members of the SDA. I hope I understood the question well. My answer is that I am certain of the last two, Ago Padzic and Mehmed Hajric, whereas I am not certain about Mr. Benjamin Kulovac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The appointment of war presidents in Zepa, was it done personally by the president of the republic, Alija Izetbegovic, or was it done by some other bodies of the government or any of the ministers?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't have that information. We always used to refer to their appointments as coming from Sarajevo. I was never a member of the party and I wasn't privy to any political processes, so I can't really respond to that. It must have been someone from the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you confirm that Mr. Hajric was also the chairman of the SDA in Zepa. Did the SDA in Zepa include any members of other ethnicities or political parties?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a small correction. I think the SDA chairman in Zepa was not Mr. Hajric. I think it was Ago Padzic. When he was removed from the position of president of War Presidency, I believe he remained in his chairman SDA position. This is what I can recall. As regards the members of the War Presidency, I did not belong to any political party, whereas for others, I don't know. There was Hurem Sakic there. I don't know whether he was an SDA member or not. I truly cannot tell you anything precisely. I don't think it was necessary for one to be an SDA member, to be a member of the War Presidency. However, most of the members were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 4258, lines 7 to 10, of the 23rd of August, you explained that Mr. Hajric was a "hodja," a cleric. That was his training. At page 4259 of the same day, lines 10 to 13, you say that the position of the president of the War Presidency was supposed to have been held by the municipal speaker, the municipal president, who was Mehmed Hajric. He was the person number one in Zepa. Given that this is unclear, was he also both the municipal president and the president of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll go back to the beginning. Given that there had been no municipal structures in existence, there were no other positions than the position of the president of the War Presidency, and he was only that. There was no other person to fill the position of the mayor or the municipal president. This was a joint function, a joint position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When Mr. Hajric was elected president of the War Presidency, given the fact that he was also a cleric, did this, as a matter of fact, mean joining the clerical and laymen's or civil powers together?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Hajric, as you say, was not a cleric in Zepa. He was a "hodja," however, not a church leader. Before the war, he had worked in a different village. In Zepa, there had been a "hodja," and he was there throughout the war as well performing that function. As far as I know, he had been a "hodja" in Podzeplje, and once the war broke out, he ended up in Zepa, like I did. In any case, he did not act as a Zepa "hodja," because there was another person during the war doing the same thing, and this was the same person who had been there before. Hajric simply did not do that part of the work at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When he was president of the War Presidency, did he also act as "hodja"?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never did. This was his vocation, so to say, but he acted as "hodja" in a completely different place before 1992. He had his own mosque. When the war broke out, he arrived in Zepa, and there was another "hodja" in Zepa who remained in that position throughout the war. They only referred to Hajric as "hodja" because that was his vocation. However, during the war he was never a "hodja" in Zepa. There was another person there who had been there for some 10 years prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this, please: Did the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajric, keep in touch with any UNPROFOR representatives and other international organisations? Did he also perform that task, since you said as follows: The War Presidency was supposed to decide on all issues concerning the life in the enclave? This is what you said in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically concerning Mr. Hajric, I can tell you that as far as I recall, he was in that position less than six months. Namely, at that time there was a problem concerning his appointment, and he did not want to assume that position. And for a month or two, Zepa did not have a person acting in capacity of the War Presidency president. A few months before Zepa finally fell, he accepted the position, so he remained in it only for a short period of time. I basically don't even recall any of his contacts with UNPROFOR, the military observers, or anyone else. He came in the end, a few months before the end, before Zepa fell.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's clarify how mayors or presidents of the War Presidency were elected in Zepa. Could we please have 1D268. It's a letter sent by the Assembly speaker of Zepa, sent to Alija Izetbegovic on the 31st of December, 1995. We are about to see it. You are probably familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I won't read it out loud. You can remind yourself, and then I will have a few questions. Please zoom in. This is dated the 13th of December, 1995, sent by the then speaker of the Assembly in Zepa, Mr. Cardakovic, to the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this document is really illegible. Is there any way to make it more legible? Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have hard copies for the witness, and it's also on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Is there a translation available? We just got the revised list of cross-examination exhibits, I guess, about 10 minutes ago, so I haven't had a chance to print anything out, look at anything. If there's a translation, it would be helpful for us. We've had no notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm told that there is no translation yet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no translation. I will read out a portion of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think your proposal to hand over a hard copy of that document to the witness would be a helpful way. That should be done.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Tolimir also be asked to read slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, but while reading, very slow, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm reading from the second paragraph: "The president of the War Presidency of Zepa municipality, Efendija Hajric, Mehmed, is requested to do as follows: At a meeting of the Assembly of Zepa, held on the 30th of December, 1994, there was discussion about a query sent to the president of the B and H Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, by the newly-appointed War Presidency president of the municipality of Zepa, Hajric, Mehmed, who has still not assumed his functions." And there has been no reply to the query sent on the 6th of November, 1994, comprising seven items. Could we please scroll up. Further down so we can see the last portion. Even more, please. Thank you. And then he continues to say, and I will now read the eighth paragraph: "... the exercise of the said function and the work of the organs of the municipality. Therefore, we request that you reply to our queries earlier as soon as possible because the situation is very serious." And now I will read the third paragraph from the bottom: "We request that the competent service of the armed forces at the Communications Centre, and in particular General Enver Hasanovic [as interpreted], to forward this communication, together with a query, directly and personally to the president of the R BiH, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and to inform us thereof." Thank you. And then we see this text. It is signed "C. Cardakovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, you've just seen this text. And could you tell us, please, why this request was sent to Alija Izetbegovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will just make a short introduction. I do remember this particular incident. That's what I've already mentioned, and maybe I wasn't clear enough. There was a problem with Mr. Mehmed Hajric accepting the role of the presidents of the municipality, and as far as I recall, he actually declined that offer. And then what followed was all this, the letter sent off. And why they were sent to the president, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, I really don't know. Maybe that was the practice in those days. I don't know if there were some other organs where these were sent, as far as the political aspects were concerned, where communications of this type would be sent. So that's all I would have to say. Now, as we can see in this particular letter, the problem surrounding the appointment of the president of the War Presidency was something that they felt they needed to inform the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was he -- as president of the War Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was he authorised to appointment all other wartime presidencies of municipalities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was -- how exactly it was done, but as far as this particular aspect is concerned, it was something that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic actually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was Mr. Hajrulahovic [as interpreted] therefore appointed by the president, Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. I've never seen any paper saying that, and I can't really say, yes, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic did that. But that he did have influence over who was going to be appointed, yes, and I believe that his decision was the final decision. Of course, I assume that somebody would have prepared all the documents and all elements that were necessary for such a decision for the president, but he was the one who would have made the decision. But there must have been other people who would actually prepare all of that in advance for the president.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us have a look at the top of this document, please, on the screen. I note we see a date, 31st of December, 1994. In the transcript, on page 7, line 8, there's a reference to the 13th of December of the next year, 1995. Perhaps Mr. Tolimir misspoke. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just one, I think, minor transcript correction. There's a reference, at LiveNote page 10, to a Mr. Hajrulahovic, who is a high-level officer within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I'm not sure that's to whom General Tolimir was referring. I suspect it was either him misspeaking or just a problem with the transcript. But if we could correct that just so there's no confusion later on. The individual whose name is there is also known as Talijan, and I think we're talking about two completely different people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, you were referring, in line 8 of page 10, to Mr. Hajrulahovic. Was that the person you mentioned or did you refer to another person in your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I can't really recall whether I mentioned that name, but the reference here was to Enver Hadzihasanovic, because we can see that name in the third paragraph from the bottom of this document. And we can see, from this decision, that Hajric was actually waiting for his official appointment by Alija Izetbegovic to this post of wartime president. And I would appreciate it if we -- I would like to tender this document into evidence because it shows that he actually exercised the duties of wartime president in an official capacity and formally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, does that clarify your concern about the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That does, Mr. President, and I hope my intervention didn't throw us off track from your question to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think both corrections are now on the transcript. Before we decide on the document, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. Just a clarification, actually. What's the difference between a cleric and a "hodja"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this particular case, we could equate them, actually. Those two terms mean the same thing. "Hodja" is one of the titles for clerics, Muslim clerics. That would be one of the levels that you can reach in your career. But in this particular case, as far as I'm concerned, you can just equate these two terms. They are the same thing to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D268 will be Exhibit D93, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I would like to let the Defence know it would be helpful for the other party, the Prosecution, to be informed a little bit earlier about use of a document and not just before trial. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise, once again, for being late in disclosing these documents. We will do our best to avoid that in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, during our conversation last week, we discussed the document on appointments of the presidents of war presidencies. Now, could you tell us what that function entails?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during my earlier testimony, I already spoke about that. As a matter of principle, the president of the Wartime Presidency is the most important individual in a certain town or area. That is the person who co-ordinates the work of everyone else, individuals and organisations, the executive committee, the civilian police, the civilian protection. Next, that title meant that he would be the person responsible for communications with international organisations and their representatives and with UNPROFOR. So, generally speaking, those would be the main functions of the president of the Wartime Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just told us that this was the most important official. Now, could you tell us what his authorities were vis-a-vis the army and military operations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your -- in my answer, my earlier answer, you could see that I did not make any mention of the army. At this time, there was a dilemma in Zepa, and this dilemma was never resolved. The dilemma was the following: whether the Wartime Presidency or, more specifically, its president was also the most responsible person for the army or was the army part of the overall military system, so that the civilian authorities would have no effective influence over any decisions that related to military matters. Now, this matter was also something that caused some personal misunderstandings between the individuals who were in these two positions, the commander of the army and the war president -- War Presidency president. Now, in this very small community, where the Wartime Presidency was in charge of organising the civilian aspects of life, but then, at least in the latter days in Zepa, there was a brigade that was part of other military structures and the chain of command was a different chain of command. Again I have to restate this, this matter was never cleared up and it was never quite clear who actually had precedence, who the boss was, the leading individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to clarify this further, could you please tell us the following: When military decisions were made, where Avdo Palic was not bound to act according to orders from the BH Army, did he, himself, make those decisions, and were they made at sessions of the War Presidency; in other words, even matters that related to military issues? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: Such instances were very few, or at least I cannot recall them. As of 1993 or up until 1993, the army was nonexistent; at least formally, it did not exist. And toward the end of 1994 and in early 1995, that is what happened then. Now, as for the decisions, I think -- I think that Colonel Palic, himself, was the person who had the greatest influence when such decisions were concerned. Now, whether there were any other arrangements that I was not privy to, I don't know. But judging by some matters that occurred in 1995, I know that Colonel Palic was almost exclusively the person who made decisions on military issues. So there was not any major influence from the president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In that case, did the Wartime Presidency have any influence over the army? And if so, what kind of influence was it? And could you tell us, please, whether there were any -- whether there was any military presence in Zepa or not? You've just told us that there wasn't, but let's talk about this as it was, actually, the realities of it.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will try to throw some further light on this. Well, there was some influence, for sure, but not -- it wasn't crucial. And let me stress, once again, that as far as I can recall, as of May 1993, up until the end of 1994, December of 1994, when I said there was no military presence, what I meant was that there didn't exist the real organised activities that are characteristic of army activities. There were people who lived in Zepa, who were organised and perhaps registered as members of the certain units, but there were no activities of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, since we've now described, up to a point, the relationship between the War Presidency and the military, my question is this: Was the Wartime Presidency duty-bound to implement the decision that would be made by the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its government? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be logical to assume, but I don't really remember that there were many such orders. But speaking within the legal framework, yes, of course, there is no dilemma as to that. If you are part of a system, then, of course, you have to implement the decision -- the decisions that are made higher up. But I tried to recall whether there was anything that we, as the Wartime Presidency, received from Sarajevo, as we used to put it, and I don't remember that there was anything like that. But as for the general aspect, my answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If the federal government issued a decision concerning the military in Zepa, was the War Presidency in charge of implementing it? Were there any dual chains that were followed or was it only the War Presidency that was in charge?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say because I can't rely on any examples. Anything related to the army arrived from the army. I don't recall a single case when we, as the War Presidency -- I think the federation came into being in 1994. When we received something, that would be related to the army. Had we received any such thing, we would have probably -- dot, dot, dot. I can tell you again that I don't remember any such thing, but, within any case, in the system of functioning, it would have been logical for us to implement the decisions of our political authorities in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Specifically, if a decision was made on a general call-up in the federation by the minister, was Zepa also tasked with implementing it; i.e., its War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is, yes, Zepa was part of that political and geographical hold. There is nothing in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether those in the War Presidency from the army, the police, and civil defence, as well as the executive board, were obliged to carry out the decisions of the Zepa War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, in principle, yes, of course, although all of the decisions we made had been previously agreed upon. And logically speaking, I'd say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the War Presidency, in the spring of 1995, informed that there was a general offensive underway of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? And if so, did they undertake the necessary measures within the enclave to support that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not recall any such notification arriving from the political structures in Sarajevo. I remember what came from the army, though. As for any political structures from Sarajevo, I don't recall ever receiving anything. As for some military orders, I do remember some.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, on page 20 of the 23rd of August this year, you said, I quote: "There were lines of communication. The most important things were also put before the War Presidency. Still, some key issues, as well as commands within the military organisations, that is something that Commander Palic received through his own lines of command and not from the War Presidency in Zepa." Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You seem to be saying that some things arrived through the War Presidency and governmental organs and other things came through Palic. Would they ever in contravention?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, I wasn't precise enough when I said that. As regards physical communication, there was only one way to do that, which was, so to say, owned by the army. It provided direct links to the military and the political structures in Sarajevo. When I said that, I had in mind a specific case. I don't recall any special orders or instructions which we, as the War Presidency, received from Sarajevo that were sent by our political authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this: Did Avdo Palic inform the War Presidency of some tasks he received where he needed to engage civilians who, of course, fell under the competence of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember and as far as I think I already testified, most of such activities, if Avdo had to do anything, Colonel Palic, that is, he didn't frequently, if I may say so, inform the members of the War Presidency. He did on one occasion, though, in the spring of 1995. It was the order to undertake certain military activities outside the enclave. I recall that. As for any previous activities, as far as I remember, such things were never on the agenda of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have 1D264 shown in e-court. It is a letter by Avdo Palic, sent to General Hadzihasanovic, brigadier-general, and to Brigadier Naser Oric on the 13th of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see it on the screen. I will quote, since it is rather illegible, and then you can confirm, perhaps: "Infantry Chetnik forces are kept under constant supervision along the entire line of the zone of responsibility. Firing positions Vrtoce, Stoborani, and Rujiste, can intercept any sabotage incursions. I would appreciate any effort made by the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the planning of any activities. What would be your suggestions if we took, by force, the weapons stored with UNPROFOR and engage in our own battle? If there is no information forthcoming, I would be forced to seize any opportunity to use small groups to make as many attacks -- carry out attacks against enemy axes." He keeps referring to UNPROFOR in the rest of the letter. My question to you is this: He seemed to have a question for Sarajevo. He basically wanted to know whether he needed to await any further UNPROFOR observer activities and whether they were informed of the situation. He also asked for further instruction. The document is signed by Avdo Palic. What personal battles or incursions is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I saw these documents three years ago when I testified in another case. There's nothing I can tell you about this. I simply don't know. This was obviously an army matter. It is possible that in late 1994, there were military activities by the VRS and that the situation was a bit tense, more than usual. However, I don't recall that there was any psychosis, the feeling of the final battle coming up. This is something we didn't have at that time. This was simply a letter sent by Mr. Palic to his superiors. I see it for the first time. I don't remember such ambiance, such atmosphere, at the time in late 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just, again, to make sure the record is as clear as possible. And I sense we're done with the document, but just when we go back in the future, the general's question referred to an inquiry of Sarajevo. He may have misspoke, and I think it's clear that this document, itself - I don't have a translation - refers to, I believe, the General Staff which was based in Kakanj, which is consistent with what the witness has testified before, the military being based in Kakanj, the political leadership being based in Sarajevo. I just wanted to clarify that for the record. I don't think there will be any dispute from the Defence about that, but I just wanted to make that clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we go back to the top of this document. And, Witness, would you confirm what the Prosecutor just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. The political centre was in Sarajevo, and the Main Staff or the General Staff, whatever the name was, of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had its headquarters in Kakanj. This is what I mentioned previously. And this is confirmed by the letter, itself, because it was sent to the command post in Kakanj, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I ever said anything to the contrary. We can see the heading, and we see therein who was at what location. Avdo Palic sent this to the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, their command post in Kakanj, Brigadier-General Enver Hadzihasanovic, who was the chief of staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to the Operational Group 8 Command of Srebrenica, Mr. Naser Oric, who was his immediate superior. I never said anything otherwise. By your leave, I'd like to put the next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are on this document, tell us this: In December 1994, when this letter was written, did the War Presidency consider the option of seizing arms from UNPROFOR, and did Avdo Palic want to do this by himself, without the knowledge of other members of the War Presidency, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this, please: In December 1994, as is stated here, did Avdo Palic carry out any consultations with the War Presidency, and how did he inform the War Presidency that he was to send sabotage groups towards Sokolac and other locations, because this must have had an impact on other military activity in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that either. I don't know whether there are any documents in existence to that effect. In late 1994, I don't seem to recall any official discussions at the War Presidency sessions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know anything about the sending of sabotage groups towards Sokolac and Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the case I already testified about. I'm trying to rewind to see whether I heard some things later, but this is the only case I can actually confirm. It was in June or July 1995. I don't know anything about this, though.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D266 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In it, on the 13th of December, 1994, Avdo Palic urgently sent a request to the Operational Administration of the command post in Kakanj, this letter. He wanted information -- or, rather, he informed the Operational Administration of the following: He says: "We are hereby sending information --" We can see it well now. This concerns the situation in the brigade. I will quote the second paragraph, staffing levels of the brigade. It says that they have 100 per cent staffing levels, in terms of manpower. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He then follows it up by saying that 30 per cent of those carry automatic weapons, and that they have 20.000 rounds, 2 mortars, 15 shells, 10 hand-held rocket-launchers, as well as 2 hand-held rocket-launchers of a different type, and that every day there are 120 soldiers on the lines. This was in December 1994. My question is this: Concerning this information about the staffing levels of the brigade and its daily activities, was the War Presidency informed of it as well, because you were a member of it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were definitely not privy to these details. We were never briefed about such issues by Colonel Palic during our sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, did you know where the army was stationed and whether there were special facilities to house them? In other words, when they were not on the front-line, where were they accommodated, where were they located, or was it the case that they actually stayed at their own houses? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no barracks in Zepa or that type of military installation. But Avdo did have two offices at his disposal. They were at the same -- in the same building where the executive committee was. The building was in down-town Zepa. And when the army was engaged in operations we see here in late 1994, that it was engaged on a daily basis on the front-lines, that there were 120 men sent to the front-line every day. I will not make any remarks regarding this. But once they were -- when they were not on the front-line, they would go home. So there was -- there were no facilities, no barracks or anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We may remove this document. Or, rather, scroll it up so that we can see the last two paragraphs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see here, in the paragraph before last, in line 3, "the defence of the free territory," and then it says: "We should use to the maximum the lay of the land by blocking the main communications that are passable by armoured and mechanised units of the enemy and, by using our main forces on those axes, prevent the enemy to breach the free territory. In addition, by infiltrating smaller sabotage groups deep behind the enemy lines, we should caress enemy units and, at critical points, ask for co-ordination with part of units of the 8th OG." And in the end, it says a number of units should be held at the ready in order to take up the weapons -- or, rather, in order to confiscate the weapons from the Ukrainian Company and in order to prevent them from leaving Zepa. Thank you. Now, could you tell us, please, how are we to interpret this letter of Avdo Palic's where he says that they should launch attacks from the demilitarised zone and keep harassing enemy troops? How did that -- what kind of effect did that have on the security of the base, of this area, because this area had the status of a demilitarised zone, and is there anything else that you can tell us about this decision of the War Presidency? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you already at the outset that this is the first time that I have seen this document, and all I can say, in answer to your questions, is this: This was not something that was discussed at any session of the War Presidency, and I think that the position of most members of the War Presidency at the time was not in favour of -- or, rather, the members of the Wartime Presidency were not in favour of these proposals that we see here by Avdo Palic, in other words, to send sabotage groups to infiltrate the enemy territory and so on, because that just exacerbated the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During your testimony on the 23rd of July [as interpreted], you said that in spring 1993, up until the spring of 1995, the enclave was shelled for reasons that had nothing to do with the enclave, itself. On page 4285 of the transcript of 29th of July, 1995 [as interpreted], you said the following, and I quote: "During that time, as far as I can recall, there were occasional shellings of the Zepa enclave, and I believe that the shelling always came as a response to some developments outside of the enclave, and what I'm saying here is, according to what I can remember, there were no attacks or any infantry advances at this time." So we are discussing the period between the spring of 1993 and the spring of 1995. Did I quote your words correctly?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my next question: Was it possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we have to check whether the dates you were referring to are correct. You were referring to the testimony of this witness of the 23rd of July. If I recall correctly, the witness was here on the 23rd of August, this month. And then later on you are referring to a transcript page of the 29th of July, 1995. I think that could be a mistake as well. Please check it and tell us the exact reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. You're absolutely right, and I will repeat this portion for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During your testimony of 23rd of August, you said that in the period between the spring of 1993 and the spring of 1995, and also in your last sentence you said on page 4285 of the transcript of 23rd, and in place of "July" it should read "August," 1995 [as interpreted], you say the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, stop. Are you really referring to 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. That should be "2010." Thank you. The testimony was in 2010. Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it on the record. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we have this little interlude, it looks like we're moving on to other exhibits. I'm just keeping my own little list here. I don't know if 1D264 and 1D266 were intended to be tendered or not, but -- before we get too far afield. Maybe I missed it, but my list shows that they haven't been offered, and I just wanted to point that out for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is our recognition as well, they were not tendered yet. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can the witness just answer this one question, and then we can go back to that issue. So my question was this: Was it possible that the shelling came as a result of some reasons that you were not privy to, as a member of the War Presidency, because you were not informed on a daily basis by Avdo Palic on the activities of the Zepa Brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, if there are no objections, I would like to tender these documents into evidence. Thank you. That's 1D266 and 1D264. Thank you. And then I will move on to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, do you want --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Both documents will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D264 will be Exhibit D94, marked for identification. 65 ter 1D266 will be Exhibit D95, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please pull up in e-court D255.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction: D55, page 3 in the English and B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat the number. That's D55, page 3 in B/C/S, or perhaps I've been misunderstood. We need the Exhibit D55, page 3 both in the English and B/C/S versions. This is an expert report by Viktor Bezruchenko, and the title is "The Fall of Zepa." And we are reading from the part where it says "Military Narrative." Could we see paragraph 8, please, and I would like to refer you to the last sentence. We have before us paragraph 4. We need paragraph 8. Thank you. That's page 3, paragraph 3 [as interpreted]. Thank you. Perhaps the witness can read through paragraph 8. This is a description of the Zepa situation and the situation within the Zepa Brigade, as described by the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will now just refer you to this part: "This strategy has shown absence of professional military planning and it defied reality on the ground and military logic and, therefore, was a harbinger of a coming disaster." This is what this expert said about the situation in Zepa. My question for the witness: Was it necessary to be told about this by a military expert or could you, yourself, actually see this for yourself on the ground?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I don't know what strategy you're referring here. I believe the strategy that is referred to is what is written in fine print there, in that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. You may, if you like, read out that portion to yourself. That's where he speaks about infiltrating groups behind enemy -- behind the Serb lines, and that's what I quoted earlier.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said this in my earlier testimony. Zepa was completely surrounded, and if you look at the number of troops, ammunition available, and weapons that they had at their disposal, in other words, if there had been a serious organised attack, Zepa would not have been able to defend itself, Zepa, itself, if you take it out of context, Zepa, without any assistance from anywhere else. So this, what we can read here, and what Colonel Palic said, although I'm no military expert, but it's all a question of what kind of resources you have. Now, if you have a limited number of bullets, for instance, you can use them up in 15 minutes, for instance. So if you don't have a normal supply line and logistics, I don't know what kind of military strategy could be sufficient to defend Zepa, if that had to be done, only based on their own internal forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, was it necessary to launch attacks from the Zepa enclave, attacks on a far stronger enemy, thereby jeopardising the status of the enclave as a demilitarised zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said this during my testimony three and a half years ago, and I said it a few days ago, that most members of the Presidency did not agree with that tactic because it -- militarily, it could not produce any effects. And, in fact, by doing so, you were just providing an excuse for the Serbian side so that it can open fire on the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that also unjustified because there were no attacks, as you said a little earlier, in the period between the spring of 1993 and the spring of 1995? So you said that there were no attacks, so was it necessary to launch attacks on the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I answered your question with my previous answer. There was no need for any such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that Avdo Palic, when he resorted to this type of strategy, relied and counted on NATO help, because no one would want to do things that would harm themselves?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I cannot say either way. But there were a few such actions, and they were not logical, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. During the examination-in-chief, you said that the War Presidency was against attacks being launched from within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little more about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a reference to an order that had arrived, and I think I was shown that order three and a half years ago when I testified here. I think it was a Defence exhibit. It referred to the period of June 1995, and I think that the situation was -- that the situation was worsened at the time. We received this order from the War Presidency, and Avdo Palic actually did these things, although we were against it. And that's what I said, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, during the examination-in-chief, you said on a number of occasions that there were instances of supplying weapons by helicopter, and ammunition, to Zepa. This is something that you said on pages 4277 and 4288 [as interpreted] of the transcript, and you said that in response to Judge Nyambe's question on 4288 [as interpreted], in line 7 through 18 -- to 12. You've said the following, I quote: "These were BH Army helicopters, or, rather, the then BH Army. These deliveries of weapons and everything else were done by the BH Army, whereby they supplied their units in Zepa and Srebrenica." Thank you. Did I quote your words correctly?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D63 shown next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you look at page 30 of today's transcript, line 17, there's a reference to pages 4277 and 4288. I think that should be corrected. I suppose you mean 4277 and 4278. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Mr. President. I thank you for your correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D63, please. It is the final analysis of the air-lift in Srebrenica and Zepa of the 17th of February, 1996, by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina Air Force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see the document. It says "Final Analysis of the Srebrenica and Zepa Air-Lift." It is stated that it was drafted by the Department for Cryptographic Data Protection on the 17th of February, 1996, that is to say, after Zepa's fall. Hence, we can say that you are being shown now a document which was produced on the 17th of February, 1996, after Zepa's fall. Since it was after Zepa's fall, could you please comment, together with me, on the document?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the heading, it says "the 17th of February, 1996," whereas just further down, it says "17 February 1995." Is there a mistake somewhere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we should blow up this part a little bit further so that we can check it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps someone was wrong about the year.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The date of production probably is the 17th February 1995. It says "Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Command of the Air Force." However, the Communications Centre forwarded this document in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see that it is divided by the line?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, although it did strike me strange because exactly one year happened between the two dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought we had agreed on what I think we can conclude from looking at the charts, themselves, that this document must have been created sometime after May of 1995, given that it details at least one flight to Zepa of 7 May 1995. So I thought we were all in agreement that the document, itself, was probably created on 17 February 1996 and forwarded on the same date, and that as we all are want to do when we're in a new year, we forget that we're in a new year and we put the old year's date. But I don't want to testify, but I thought we sort of shared that understanding about the date disparity here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This matches with my recollection. But in February, you normally know you're in the new year. I think to clarify this also for the witness, we should have a look at that part you were referring to, Mr. Thayer, where there is mention of an occurrence of May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's page 10 of e-court in the English, and let me just count the pages for the B/C/S. I think page 10 of the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In B/C/S, it is obviously the wrong page, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Page 11 of the B/C/S, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's clear what it's referring to, an occurrence in May 1995. So everybody agrees this document was produced in 1996, in February. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As was just said, in this document, in attachment 2 on page 11 in Serbian and page 10 in English, we have an overview of the sorties to Zepa and the amount of supplies carried, as well as some other information. Please have a look. You can see it on the screen, I believe.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the right column -- sorry, in the second column, it says "Months," that is to say, in what month things were delivered or supplied. Does this correspond to what you know about the helicopter flights coming from Tuzla or Kakanj or federation territory to Zepa; that is to say, the flights which took the helicopters across the territory of Republika Srpska and into the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know about the number of flights, I can tell you that this tallies. There were about 10 flights before a helicopter was shot down. As for the transfer of materiel and equipment, I can't tell you about quantities. I do know that on a number of occasions, they also carried some officers and people, as I can see here next to the column identifying the amount of actual supplies. I also remember that it was in early May, and here I can see the date of the 7th of May when the helicopter was shot down. That was the last flight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would that be a convenient time for the first break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I certainly do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have our first break now, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At page 4277 on the transcript of the 23rd August 2010, lines 6 to 10, you say as follows: "These helicopters delivered supplies mainly at night. The Serb side didn't take long to notice those helicopters' flight and begin opening fire at them, and the inhabitants of Zepa became familiar with what was being done." Given that even the inhabitants of Zepa, as well as the Serb side, were aware that there were helicopters flying about, did UNPROFOR know anything about them, as far as you know.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already answered that in my testimony. I truly don't know. I can repeat what I do know. Avdo was in charge of all UNPROFOR contact at the time. The only thing I can say is that it would have been illogical for them not to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning these helicopter flights at night, did UNPROFOR discuss this with anyone; say, the War Presidency? Did they ever protest with the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any discussions or protests made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the inhabitants of Zepa concerned, once they noticed these helicopters flying, because they could reasonably expect that military activities would follow?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to recall what their reactions were, although I did have contact with other inhabitants of Zepa. In any case, quantitatively speaking, these were not large deliveries. If one looks at it from a certain point of view, you could conclude that this could have two sides to it. One was the hope that Zepa would finally be able to defend itself, and the second one could be a reason for concern because of the violation of the agreement that had been signed. I don't remember any precise reactions by Zepa inhabitants. It was quite a long time ago. Please understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During examination-in-chief, you mentioned the helicopter that was shot down. Could we please have 1D251 shown. So that based on Avdo Palic's report, you could comment. This is an information of the 6th of July -- sorry, between the 6th and the 7th of July --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Between the 6th and the 7th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is when the helicopter was actually shot down. Perhaps you could have a look and then comment.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to read it, although I can barely make it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see, in the second paragraph, that: "The following were killed in the helicopter accident"?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says "Azim Becirovic, Ramiz Becirovic, Ejub Golic, Mehmet Alic, Samir Karic, Cebo Djeric [phoen]."

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we scroll up, please, in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Numo Krluc, a certain Cardakovic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know of these people, and can you tell us who is Ejub Golic, who is Ramiz Becirovic, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have some people from Zepa and Srebrenica here. I know the people from Zepa, when I read the names on the list. The ones I don't know are from Srebrenica. If you wish, we can go one by one and I can tell you who is from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's start with the first wounded person, Ramiz Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Any Ejub Golic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Hamed Malic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mehmed Malic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Samir Karic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He might be from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Emir Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dzevad Dzananovic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the doctor who went from Tuzla to Srebrenica, so he was not from Srebrenica, nor from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dzebo?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The next person?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Numo Krluc?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You also see the persons who were killed, and I believe they are also people from Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many were from Zepa and how many from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might not be precise, but I'll try. The first three were the helicopter crew. It just went off the screen. I don't see the list anymore. Could you please put this list back on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. We wanted to see the last names on the list in B/C/S you were referring to. And now we go back to the first page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was whether among those killed, were there any from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica or Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among those killed, if I look at the last names, there were one or two from Zepa. The rest were not from Zepa. So there were three crew members. Then there were three doctors who went from Tuzla to Srebrenica. Then one or two people were returning to Zepa, and the rest -- well, two or three could be from Zepa, I guess. Homarac could be from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that we have people from both Zepa and Srebrenica, as far as you know, why did they travel jointly to Tuzla and going back together to Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early 1995, there was an initiative, I don't know whether from Srebrenica or from Zepa -- well, it was actually initiated by the General Staff, and a certain number of officers went to the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina for training and retraining. After a while, they returned to Srebrenica and Zepa. I don't know whether there were also some civilians who were returning, but basically these were all officers who had undergone training with the Main Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir speak closely to the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please take the microphone a little bit more into your direction. Turn the microphone a little bit towards you, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, please -- there were some individuals for Srebrenica, and there were also some from Zepa. Did they meet at the War Presidency, and did the UNPROFOR know about their arrival there and whether they had any contact with the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is your question whether these individuals from Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, yes, had a meeting with one of the members of the War Presidency or some of the members.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had a meeting with them. At the time when they were supposed to travel, I think this was in winter in early 1995, I had a brief meeting with Naser Oric. He was waiting for this flight, and he came to see me, asking for assistance to the civilians of Srebrenica. He asked me whether we had some stocks of flour because the food situation in Srebrenica was very difficult. So I recall that one meeting. That was sometime before these people left. The meeting was brief, perhaps 15 minutes or so. And that is what I can confirm. Now, whether these people had a meeting with some other members of the War Presidency, I really don't know, but there was no official meeting with the War Presidency where these people would be attending as guests. But I do confirm that I had a meeting with Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did these people stay while they were waiting for the flight, and did the UNPROFOR know anything about the helicopter flights or not?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I don't even think they came to Zepa. They were in the mountains where the helipad was, a temporary helipad. Whether the UNPROFOR knew anything about it, I really don't know. That's my answer. I don't know if they knew about these people being there. But as far as I can remember, they had to wait some five to six days for the helicopter to land because of the weather conditions and so on. You know, the conditions were very complex, and it was difficult to determine the time of the helicopter flight.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now pull up D67, please, in e-court. D67. This is a document dated 13 of July, 1997, by General Rasim Delic. He's sending a communication to General Hajrulahovic, and with a request that he forward it to the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we go on, I would like to tender the previous document into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D251 will be Exhibit D96.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the witness to take a look at paragraph 6 of the document we have before us in e-court, the paragraph which begins with the words: "For training ..." And I will read it: "Preparing for the future operation of joining the enclaves, we brought back and returned for brigade commanders two chiefs of staffs of brigades and the 26th Division chief of staff. The division commander who was meant to go on the next helicopter flight did not return after the final flight ended tragically, Naser remained."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind what we've just read, tell us, please, what reference is this to an operation to link up the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, and did you, as a member of the Presidency, have any knowledge about this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, pursuant to this document in paragraph 2, as far as that period was concerned, this information here is incorrect. There were not 17 helicopter flights, but 10 only, and only 1 of them was downed. That's just something that I would like to comment on just by perusing this document. Now, as for the operation to link up the enclaves, I don't know anything about that, nor did that make any sense, in military terms. I can give you my opinion on this, but I don't know whether the person who drafted this document -- I don't know whether it's an order or a report, but I don't know how well this person knew the situation. The enclaves at that time were very small and close to each other and you could walk from one to the other, so there was no military sense in trying to link them up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, could we just scroll the document up a little bit so that we can see the bottom of it and the author of this document. That's right. Could you please go on a little further. We just want the date to be shown. Could you please -- could you please scroll it up a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, here we see this document was drafted by the General Staff of the Army, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the 13th of July, which means after the fall of the enclave, and this is a report sent to the commander, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency. And now if we can look at the last page so we see who signed this document. Thank you. Here, we see it was drafted by Army General Rasim Delic, commander. He reports on the deliveries that were made, all the things that we've seen in the previous document. In other words, this document was signed by Army General Rasim Delic, and he reports to the president on the supplies provided to Zepa. Now, if he, as the army commander, mentions the link-up of the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, in military terms, does that mean, maybe, that militarily they had a plan of which you, members of the War Presidency, knew nothing about?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they did have any plan, I didn't know about it. Now, again, if I think about it logically, I don't see what they could link up. Maybe this refers to some activities to expand or enlarge the corridor. But we, in any case, did not know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see all the supplies that arrived in Srebrenica. Now let's take a look at page 2. Yes, we have it now. Can we please just enlarge it a bit so the witness can read it. Here, you can see the columns headed "Zepa" and "Srebrenica." The first one is "Zepa," the second "Srebrenica," and the third says "Totals." So you can see, for instance, that 106 rifles were delivered, RPG 7/8, 107 rockets, 12 pieces, and so on and so forth. You can also take a look at the next page to see the supplies that reached Zepa. The first column is Zepa. There, you can see that all these items were delivered. Can you tell us whether this actually confirms that weapons and ammunition were sent to the enclave even after it was demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I can say, of course, is that I know nothing about these quantities and whether the information contained therein is correct. But as for the time when this -- these deliveries were made, we could see that it was in late 1994 and up until mid-May 1995, so that would be the period referred to therein.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please -- I would like to tender this into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now I would like us to see 1D263. This is a document dated the 9th of March, 1995, and the author of the document is Naser Oric, as we can see from the document. We would just like to take a look at the last sentence, which reads as follows. Now, the document is not very clear, so I will read a portion: "For the time being, I remain in Zepa, certain that you will organise my transport to where you are very soon."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see, this document is dated the 9th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, the 9th of March. As you already mentioned, it was in winter-time. Now, do you know that Naser Oric was in Zepa at this time, and do you know how long he had to stay in Zepa and how long he had to wait for his transport to the territory of the federation, which was in Tuzla, where his command was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, I had that brief meeting with Naser Oric. Whether he remained in the center of Zepa, he, himself, all that time, I don't know. I do know that he was in the hills. But I know that he had to wait for some seven days or so for the flight, and I know that this was something that he arranged with Avdo. So I don't really know a lot about this whole affair. I just know and can confirm that I met with Naser once. We discussed the staple foods and flour that they needed, and that's all I know. He was -- at that time, he was in the center of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us, do you know whether on that occasion he met with the War Presidency and whether he attended any of the sessions of the War Presidency in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall any such instance where he was -- where he attended any session of the War Presidency. The meeting that I mentioned was in my office. There was no one else there, I think. We just talked about the flour and how best to deliver it. So I don't remember that he was at any meeting of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D263 will be Exhibit D97, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have document 1D252, please, 1D252. We're waiting for it to come up. Thank you. There, now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document sent by Avdo Palic to the brigadier, Enver Hasanovic [as interpreted], on the 28th of May, 1995, and it reads as follows, I quote, that's item 1: "Measures have been taken to seal off the area controlled by UNPROFOR and the direction of possible withdrawal. "No signs were registered of the situation deteriorating or anything that would indicate a possible withdrawal of UNPROFOR, except for their fear, to an extent, of a possible Chetnik attack." Paragraph 3: "I agreed in principle, in case of an attack, on some sort of co-ordinated action with UNPROFOR and requisitioning the weapons given to them for safekeeping." My question is this: Why were measures taken to seal off the area controlled by UNPROFOR, in view of the fact, as it says in this report, itself, that there were no signs registered of the situation deteriorating? So do you know anything about why these measures were taken? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know absolutely nothing about any measures. And looking at this letter, perhaps it was really just talk. I don't know that anything was done and whether Colonel Palic really took any action or did anything or just wrote about it to the command. I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if Colonel Palic had to take some measures that involved UNPROFOR, was he obliged to inform thereof the General Staff of the army, because they were in charge of contacts with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we think about it, logic would command that that would be required, because the War Presidency would be responsible for giving their approval for this or at least to be informed of any such measures or actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we see that mention is made in this document of some kind of general agreement with UNPROFOR. So who would be the competent person or institution to have these contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
