utterances.text: Did I understand your question correctly, who would be the liaison person in UNPROFOR? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, all the contacts went through Sejmon Dudnjik. So when Avdo says "UNPROFOR," I think he was really referring to Colonel Sejmon Dudnjik, who was the commander of the Zepa mission, the UNPROFOR Zepa mission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, and I would also like to have document D16 before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D252 will be Exhibit D98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But before this document disappears from the screen, I would like to clarify one word with the witness. What is the correct understanding of the word "Chetnik"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best to explain that. Not going into the historical background, a Chetnik is really a pejorative term used by the BH Army, Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when referring to the Serb Army. You may have noticed, during some other -- or in some other exhibits, where even General Mladic uses the term "Turks," which is a pejorative term -- derogatory term for Muslim soldiers. They referred to them as Turks. So this was the wartime terminology that was bandied about. Now, as for "Chetniks" in historical terms, that's something else, and I'm just -- I was just making a reference to the use of these terms in the last war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we should have D16 on the screen. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we wait for this document to appear, could we first take a look at the top of the document. As we can see, this is a document produced by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the General Staff of the army, and then it says "The Command Post at Kakanj" of 17 February 1992, and the title is "Taking Measures to Raise the Level of Combat Readiness." And then it says "Order." This order was issued to the Command of the 2nd Corps to the OG Srebrenica Command and the Command of the 1st Zepa Brigade.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please scroll this document down in the B/C/S so I can just take a look at it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we do that, please, for the witness's sake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could we just see the document through to the very bottom. How many items does this order contain?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, there are seven items or paragraphs on the first page under "Order." Now, we will go to the second paragraph, the paragraph beginning with the words "The aggressor ...," in B/C/S. In English, that begins with the words: "On 16 February ..." So we can see in the seventh line from the top, and I quote. It says: "On the 16th of February, 1995, the aggressor filed a request with UNPROFOR to declare Zepa a 'non-demilitarised zone,' with the following rationale: "BH Army helicopter flights supplying weapons and ammunition have been registered; "Movements of the BH Army; "Accusing members of the Ukrainian Battalion that they are covering up for the activities and intentions of the BH Army, which is why they no longer guarantee their safety." And also that: "On the night between 15 and 16 February 1995, our helicopters were seen flying over and the infantry fire was opened on them." Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you see that your army actually submits this request, and it refers to a request from the Army of Republika Srpska that Zepa be declared a non-demilitarised zone. Now, my question for you: Were you aware of this letter where the Main Staff was asking for Zepa to be declared a non-demilitarised zone, the Main Staff of your own army?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall that it was mentioned officially in any of the War Presidency meetings in Zepa. These types of letters would always go to Avdo, to Colonel Palic, but whether it was actually ever put in place, I can only say that it was never actually the subject of any discussions at the War Presidency. It wasn't on its agenda for any of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, just so we have a clear record in the future, Mr. President, again I -- perhaps General Tolimir misspoke, but I think it's clear, and I just want to see if there's any dispute on this issue, because there's no dispute from the Prosecution, looking at this document, that what it says is that the aggressor - here that would be the VRS - filed a request with UNPROFOR to have Zepa declared a non-demilitarised zone. I think we've seen this document before, and that's been the understanding. I just note that in General Tolimir's last question, he referred to this request being from the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I just -- those are two entirely different things, meaning two entirely different things. I don't think that's what the question meant to say, but I just want to clarify that for the record, because the document is quite clear and I think we've all shared that understanding. But if there is a different question, then I think we should make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I see, in page 50, line 2, a request from the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Then the problem is at the end of the question: "Now, my question for you: Were you aware of this letter where the Main Staff was asking for Zepa to be declared a non-demilitarised zone, the Main Staff of your own army." And that's where I think the lack of clarity may come to haunt us if we don't take care of it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it is clear, what you are referring to. Would you please clarify this? Is Mr. Thayer right? Was this the right interpretation of your question?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was this: Did you know that the Main Staff of the VRS sent a protest letter to UNPROFOR, asking for Zepa to be declared a non-demilitarised zone because there were certain activities underway? I apologise if I misspoke. Perhaps this should be corrected for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was only the problem of the words "the Main Staff of your own army," that obviously you're referring to the Army of the VRS. Now, Witness, could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the War Presidency of Zepa was not familiar with any such requests. If I can see it properly, this document was produced by the Main Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in one item mention is made of the request of the VRS for Zepa to be pronounced a non-demilitarised zone. Hence, my answer is that we were not familiar with this, as the War Presidency of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it customary -- or would it have been customary to inform the War Presidency and the civilian structures about the new status of Zepa, since there was a request on the table for it to be declared a non-demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, the War Presidency should have been informed. Especially, it should have been informed of all matters which had to do with the security and safety of the population in Zepa. I believe this, too, should have been discussed by the War Presidency, or at least it should have been informed of -- in Zepa. However, I must say that there was this key problem of communication here. The only communication means were in the hands of Mr. Palic. Therefore, he was free to select what he would and would not forward to anyone in the enclave. So we did not have communication channels of our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a possibility that Avdo Palic did not show this document to the War Presidency and that he did not share this information with any civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. There is such a possibility, of course. Perhaps he may have conveyed something orally to the president of the War Presidency. In any case, I don't remember this document or its contents being on the agenda of any War Presidency sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please scroll up so that we could see the specific items of this order. It is page 2 in the English. In the Serbian version, all of the items are on page 1. We see now item 1, where it says: "Bring the units of OG 8 to full combat readiness, enabling them to be fully prepared to resist a possible attack by the aggressor." These units of OG 8, did this refer to the Zepa Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: OG 8? What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The 17th of February, 1995, produced by Chief of Staff Brigade General Enver Hadzihasanovic. He sent it to the 2nd Corps Command in Tuzla and to the Command of OG 8 in Srebrenica, as well as to the Command of the 1st Zepa Brigade.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is OG 8? Well, is this part of some earlier military structure? I only know of the 285th Brigade in Zepa. I don't understand this particular terminology. I don't know what "OG 8" is. Was that a new organisational entity within the existing system or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The 28th Division of Srebrenica, could that have been OG 8 when the superior command referred to it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well be. Before the final reorganisation when the 28th Division came into being, I think there were some operational groups that were part of the corps, but I'm surprised by the date of this document. I think by that time it should have been the 28th Division, Command of the 285th East Bosnia Brigade, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at item 3. I will quote for the record, and then I have a question: "Bringing units to full combat readiness and other measures must be taken under strict secrecy in order to eliminate any grounds on the aggressor's part for violations of the agreement on the demilitarised zone (protected zone)." My question is this: Was the War Presidency supposed to co-ordinate any activity with the Zepa Brigade when undertaking these measures and with the Command in Srebrenica? What was the correlation between the Zepa War Presidency and that of Srebrenica, vis-a-vis the units in Zepa and Srebrenica and their activities?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the situation in Zepa, specifically, it would have been logical for us to do it that way. However, most of the communication and most of those measures were undertaken without the approval or without the War Presidency being informed of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have D53 in e-court. The title is "Preparation to Carry Out Offensive Combat Activities." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please zoom in. It reads: "Pursuant to a verbal order," and I underscore "verbal order, issued by the commander of the General Staff of the BH Army, Army General Rasim Delic, and on the occasion of the great success achieved by units of the BH Army in the wide area around Sarajevo and Gorazde, as well as on the basis of intelligence that the A/S Command of the Protection Regiment in Han Pijesak is holding part of its units in reserve to intervene in the event of an attack by our forces from Zepa, I hereby issue the following order: "Execute all preparations in the Command of the 28th Land/Army Division to execute offensive operations with a view to liberating the territory of BH, overextending the -- "A/S," I believe it means "aggressor forces," "and inflicting losses on them, co-ordinating action with the BH Army forces carrying out operations in the broader Sarajevo area. "2. Plan realistic tasks which will assure certain success, on the basis of an accurate assessment and the potential of our forces in Srebrenica and Zepa. "3. The General Staff of the BH Army will regulate, by an order, the commencement of offensive combat activities in the zone of responsibility of the 28th Division." It was drafted by the chief of staff of the Army of B and H on the 17th of June, 1995, that is to say, one month prior to the events we've been discussing. They sent this order to the Command of the 28th Division. It was drafted by the chief of staff of the 2nd Corps, Brigadier Budakovic. We see the addressees. The second one is the 28th -- 285th Light Brigade, Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The order you mentioned, which arrived from Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that order discussed by the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This order drafted by the General Staff of the army, sent to the 28th Division -- oh, it is in evidence already. I apologise. Could we next have Avdo Palic's letter of the 28th of June, 1995. It is D62, the 28th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this, please answer my question. In that period, in June, before the final activities in Zepa, were you, the War Presidency, informed of any Sarajevo events? And if so, how was that information passed on to you? What do you know about the military activities in Sarajevo referred to in this report, in particular those aimed at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, as far as I recall, there was an operation by the 1st Corps of the Army of B and H. It was an attempt at lifting the siege of Sarajevo. We had no official information about that, but it was publicised and it was no secret. One could hear it on the radio, TV, and in other media. We knew that at that time the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina tried to lift the siege of Sarajevo by using military means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's focus on this document. This document was drafted by the 285th Brigade from Zepa. The date is the 28th of June. It was signed by Avdo Palic, as you will see later. It was sent to the 2nd Corps Command, the chief of staff, Budakovic, and the Command of the 28th Division, to Major Ramiz Becirovic. Before I put any questions to you: Do you know who Ramiz Becirovic was, and why did Palic send this document to him? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who he is. At the time, he was the chief of staff of the 28th Division, given that the commander, Naser, was not in Srebrenica. Therefore, he was in charge of the 28th Division in his absence. It was Mr. Becirovic at the time. I don't know him personally, but I have encountered his name in some documents and I know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see what Avdo Palic put in this document. Focus on the second paragraph, where he says: "Upon receipt of the orders given to me by brigade commanders Major Zulfo Tursunovic and Major Ibrahim Mandzic, and by the assistant for intelligence in the division, Captain Ekrem Salihovic, I reviewed the overall situation with respect to this kind of combat action, and, based on earlier instructions issued to the chief of staff, Major Ramo Cardakovic, by the chief of General Staff, Brigadier-General Enver Hadzihasanovic, I decided, together with Tursunovic and Mandzic, to proceed as follows:" This is, de facto, Avdo Palic's decision, and we can read out what he decided. The next paragraph reads: "Form a number of sabotage groups of between a squad to reinforce platoon strength, and dispatch them into the temporarily-occupied territory for the purpose of inflicting on the aggressor as great losses as possible, in terms of troops and equipment, and tying him down, with the new forces he requires, on a line over 20 kilometres wide. The places of attacks and raids by the sabotage-reconnaissance platoon groups were the following:" And here we see what areas these attacks were carried out in: "Group 1: The area of Zljebovi-Pecnik (Han-Kram). "Group 2: The area of Rijeka. "Group 3: The area of Veliki Zep." You know where it is: "Group 4, the area of Solila. "Group 5, the area of Crna Rijeka, where the Main Staff was. "Group 6, the area of Banja Lucica. "Group 7, the area of Crna Rijeka, Bojcino Brdo, close to the Main Staff. "Group 8, the area of Karaula. "Group 9, the area of the village of Visenjica, attacking the units there." Please scroll up in the Serbian. We can see it now. Can we please have page 2 in the English. We have read out the groups he sent -- we will only read out the following parts. In the second paragraph, he said that all sabotage groups carried out their attacks, causing great losses to the enemy troops and equipment. In the third paragraph, he says about 40 Chetniks were killed. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And dozens were wounded: "A significant quantity of infantry weapons were seized (one M53 light machine-gun, six automatic rifles, one carbine, two radio transmitters, 5.000 rounds and other soldier's equipment). One aggressor soldier was captured in the area of Vrana Kran [phoen]. He was lightly wounded in the area of the chest. His name is Velimir Merdjan, born 1975 ... "He is now in Zepa, referring treatment," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just two quick points, Mr. President. The first is obviously, and I know we're probably sounding like a broken record on this, but there is no dispute from the Prosecution as to the attacks by ABiH forces from within the enclave of Zepa towards the outside. That, again, is not in contest from the Prosecution, and not putting any limitations on how General Tolimir wants to conduct his cross. He's entitled to take it wherever he pleases. But I just want again to make that clear that that is not in dispute. And the second thing is just a minor, I think, correction for the record. This is already in evidence, but as General Tolimir was reading through the paragraph, it's clear that some of these attacks were carried out, and some weren't. And just for the record, if you want to go back, we can see here that numbers 5, 7, 8, 9, those targets were attacked, whereas targets 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6 were not actually attacked. Again, we're not interested in the ins and outs of these. It's not a contested point. But I think in his question, again, maybe General Tolimir misspoke when he summarised this paragraph, but he did say all the attacks were carried out, and it's clear that that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was referring to the activities that were envisaged. And in the cases where he was unsuccessful, he did not report on those, but he did report on those activities where he was successful and where he even captured some prisoners of war. So he did not report on those where they were unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So my question would be this: Was it common practice for a demilitarised zone to have prisoners of war, and is the reference here to Velimir Merdjan, a prisoner of war, the same Merdjan that General Mladic mentioned on the occasion of the signing of the evacuation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I should answer two questions. First, I would like to confirm that it is, indeed, the same individual, the same soldier. I just know that his name was Merdjan, his last name. That was number 1. And, number 2, of course, it was not logical for any prisoners of war to be held in a demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At the War Presidency sessions, did you ever discuss these issues of pulling out of Zepa and also the major successes that Colonel Palic makes a reference to here?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the document is dated the end of June, and the attacks on Srebrenica and Zepa began on the 6th of July. There were no analyses made, but there was, one could already sense in Zepa, a special mood. There was an atmosphere where people were expecting for something to happen. As for the situation itself, we were not informed by Avdo of any of this. This was a report for his superior command. And very soon thereafter, the final stages were in place and -- the end game was in place, as it were. We did not discuss any of this at the War Presidency. I can just confirm that we did not discuss any of these matters at the War Presidency, and that refers also to the order from the Presidency that you mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind that sabotage operations were launched from Srebrenica and Zepa, behind the Serb lines - some of these operations targeted civilians, others army facilities - were there any discussions at the War Presidency that possibly the BH Army -- the Serb Army would try and take counter-measures in order to prevent and preempt such attacks from the demilitarised zones? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, when the War Presidency discussed at its session the order that it had received from the Command of the 285th Brigade -- or, actually, the order for the 285th Brigade, the reason why most members of the War Presidency were opposed to such an order was precisely in their expectation that the Serb Army would respond by launching an attack -- military attacks on the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now skip the warnings that General Mladic made the UNPROFOR aware of and his expectations what might happen. But I would skip all that and just would like to discuss something else with you. On page 14 of the transcript of the 23rd of August, you mentioned the role of the board, of which you were a member of, and you said that one of the roles was the distribution of humanitarian aid, and that is the issue that I would like to discuss now. Now, did Colonel Palic have any role in the distribution of humanitarian aid? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and I'm not absolutely certain that this relates to June of 1995, but I vaguely seem to remember that maybe certain quantities -- small quantities of humanitarian aid were also allocated for the army. I can't really say for sure. But in any case, the distribution of the humanitarian aid was done according to the list of inhabitants. And for every convoy of humanitarian aid that arrived, the executive committee would take a decision on the amount of humanitarian aid and items that would be distributed per inhabitant. Now, as for the question relating to Avdo, I really don't recall -- I don't have any clear recollection of that. If you have a document to show me, maybe that would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well, we'll do that. But let me ask you: Were there priorities set in the distribution of humanitarian aid, and what did those priorities actually relate to?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember if we actually had a list of priorities in distributing humanitarian aid, but I seem to remember generally that all the distributions actually were meant and were envisaged for all inhabitants; in other words, for the civilian population according to the lists compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, how did the members of the Zepa Brigade provide food for their brigade? Did they receive food supplies or did they -- so did they receive them from the civilian authorities, the War Presidency and the Executive Board, or did they just go home and eat?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, there was no organised feeding of the army, as it were. Each member of the army reached humanitarian aid as an inhabitant, a civilian of Zepa. For instance, Mujo Mujic had a four-member family, so that would mean that the family would get four times, let's say, five kilos of flour. They would get 20 kilos of flour in total. So that was the principle according to which the aid was distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to see document 1D245 in e-court. This is a letter from Mehmed Hajric of the 5th of May, 1995. He's sending a request to the Government of the Republic of Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have before us what he wrote. In line 13 from the top in the second paragraph, he says the following: "Since this would apply to about 150 such individuals, we wish to ask for your opinion on the validity of this position." And then he goes on. So he mentions here an application for 150 people. Could you tell us what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. As it says in the document, itself, most inhabitants, then inhabitants of Zepa, over 60 per cent, were not people who were born -- or had been born and lived in Zepa, they were refugees. Now, he discusses here the most difficult conditions, the people in the most difficult conditions, and that they would need to be evacuated and then taken back to their families and reunited with their families. Some of them were in Sarajevo or elsewhere. And now your question was related to that, his opinion and our opinion that these 150 people should be evacuated from Zepa or relocated from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is my question: You said about 60 per cent of the population in Zepa were refugees. Did all those 60 per cent of the people who were there -- were they all of the same opinion? Did they all want, like these 150 mentioned here, to be relocated and moved to the territory of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, most of them didn't have any family members elsewhere. Only these 150 people had members of family elsewhere. As for the rest, they were there -- entire families were there in Zepa. And at this time, the situation in Zepa was very bad, and it was the prevailing opinion that Zepa was the worst possible solution for them and that they would be better off if they were someplace else. That is true, that was the predominant feeling among most of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What was the opinion of the other 35 per cent?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the others did not want to leave. They were people who lived there. They had been born and lived there all their lives. Now, whether the percentage was 35 per cent, or 38, or 40, but generally that was the ratio, 40 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, was there a lot of pressure from the refugees who wanted to be relocated? And what kind of pressure did you feel within the Presidency, and what did you do about it, and did you get any response from the central authorities?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see the document that we still have before us, the then president of the War Presidency had contacted Sarajevo. I don't know what their response was. But this was something that we tried to resolve this situation through a welfare evacuation, as it was called then. I don't even know if there was any response from the Government of the Republic-Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please -- he says here, in the last sentence of his letter, the president of the municipal Assembly of Zepa: "Please respond and give us your response, as soon as possible, to our communication." Now, my question is this: Why this so important that he urgently requested that he be given a reply, and he referred to it as: "We kindly ask that you urgently give us the government position on these issues"? Now, were you given any kind of dead-line?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I'm sure it wasn't as dramatic as it appears. Perhaps Mr. Hajric had a desire to help these people, but there was nothing else that was especially a burning issue at the time. This trend or desire to leave Zepa was something that was in evidence constantly, so it was always something that the refugees were considering. But I don't recall that there was anything specific at this point in time that would have called for a dramatic call, as presented here in this letter by Mr. Mehmed Hajric. In any case, we see from the document that there was some discussion at the local level, with regard to this matter, with the VRC [as interpreted] officer, Pecanac, I believe. I'm not sure that I recall this particular event.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. While we still have this document before us, could you please read what it reads under A: "Is it possible at the present time to negotiate a welfare evacuation from Zepa at the local level with Serbian officer Milan Pecanac (negotiations proposed for 10 May 1995)." And under B: "Would the welfare evacuation from Zepa be justified with regard to the current military and political situation in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?" Thank you. What can you tell us about this, and was this the position taken by the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in reference to A, maybe I do recall vaguely, but I am not sure whether these negotiations with Pecanac were held. But if they were, an army officer would have had to be involved in this because, as far as I know, no civilians went to those negotiations or attended those negotiations. But, generally speaking, in wartime I don't know what the position would be on these welfare evacuations. I assume that the response from Sarajevo would be that such evacuations should be avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Hajric referred to this as welfare evacuation, and he's requesting the government and informing the government of it, and he says that he has sought contact with the Serb side. And then he says -- we can see here where he specifically says: "Would a welfare evacuation from Zepa be justified with regard to the military and political situation ..." So my question to you is this: Was this type of -- were these types of communication generally sent to the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and did you receive any response?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we can just go back to the top of the document, and you can see that everything did have to go through military channels. As a member of the War Presidency, I may have been informed of this orally, but I have never seen these documents before. The only way of communicating was by means of the military Paket radio equipment. It all depended on that. Anything that had to be forwarded had to be decided on by Colonel Palic. Any document could have been removed, because there was no possibility to check whether someone, indeed, sent it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender the document on the screen into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D99.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D246 on the screen. It is a letter of Captain First Class Salih to the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He drafted it following his commander's approval, that is to say, commander of the 2nd Corps. Could we please zoom in for the witness. We see here that he says: "We have unverified information that in the near future, a certain number of people will make an unauthorised and illegal exit from the Zepa zone, leaving through the forest towards the free territories of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina (Kladanj, Olovo)." The second paragraph: "We will undertake the necessary measures to prevent this from occurring." Third paragraph: "We therefore inform you of this and request that you bring this information to the attention of the commands of units whose zone of responsibility is in those parts of the republic, so that the members and commands of those units will know how to handle any people who may be deserters, should they not have documents issued by the command of this unit, and so that they can promptly inform us ..." It was drafted by Assistant Commander for Intelligence Salih Hasanovic, sending it to the chief of staff, General Enver Hadzihasanovic, on the 25th of May. Could this letter contain the answer that was never sent to Hajric, when he was never explained how to treat those people who wished to exit, and it was basically 65 per cent of the people that were in the enclave who did not have their homes there.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously this document indicates that there were activities underway aimed at leaving the enclave of Zepa, although this does seem a bit exaggerated when these officers referred to it. The territory of Zepa could independently be left only by those who had arms and those who were fit the most. Only those members of the army could leave who knew where the free passage route was. Women and children could not make that trip. It would include 40 kilometres of terrain crossing two lines of defence. Women and children couldn't do that. Only the best-equipped and trained members of the army could leave the enclave in this way. As for whether the wish to leave existed at the time, yes, indeed, it was the case, much as the case was with Sarajevo. People wanted to leave because they were under a siege. It's only natural they wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This request sent by the commander first class, on his commander's orders, to the Main Staff, was it aimed at preventing any departures and people leaving the enclave? Did any authorities work on preventing the civilians to leave for other areas?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, army bodies wanted to prevent any able-bodied men to leave. It would mean deserting your unit. As for the civilians, in particular women and children, in principle, it wasn't their job to do that. They had nothing to do with the civilians. As for the army, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document, 1D246, and then I will move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, before you move to another topic, we must have our second break now, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have P123 shown in e-court. It is dated 13 July 1995. It was sent to General Mladic and the command of the Drina Corps, General Krstic, to the Protection Regiment and to the Communications Regiment. It discusses the situation in Zepa, and I signed it. We can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to quote you first. At page 4289, line 25, to page 4290, line 3, you say as following: "After Srebrenica fell on the 12th of July, 1995, on the same day the War Presidency of Zepa, via UNPROFOR and Colonel Sejmon Dudnjik, received a request or an invitation for talks with the other side." My question is this: Was all that communication going through Dudnjik and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As it is stated in paragraph 1, was there an agreement for a meeting to take place at 2100 hours? It was drafted on the 13th of July, in the afternoon, and it says: "We have established planned contacts with representatives from Zepa, Toplak [as interpreted] and Imamovic. It was arranged previously to meet around 9:00 p.m. We were advised by UNPROFOR that during the day, they were busy consulting with the inhabitants about the conditions of moving out of Zepa and that they were forced to do that due to the decision made by the government in Sarajevo, which stated that they should not move. They advised most of the population and soldiers that they would be granted safe passage or stay in the area of Zepa if they surrendered their weapon and recognised the Serb authority." Is it true that you were unable to attend that meeting because of the activity specified herein?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I wouldn't say that there was an arrangement made. Rather, it was requested by your side that the meeting took place around 9.00 p.m. As I said before, first we sought approval from our political and military leadership to be granted leave to talk to you at the local level. I believe during my testimony here, I said that clearly. I said that the request or query was sent to our political and military leadership, asking whether we were allowed to engage in any talks with the Serb side at the local level. I must also say that at the meeting of the War Presidency in Zepa, we did not discuss the things specified in this report, as far as I remember, such as that the population of Zepa should be removed immediately, if they wished to do so, transferred elsewhere. What I remember was that we had a lengthy War Presidency meeting, and at the very beginning we forwarded that question to our political leadership to see whether we were allowed to engage in any talks. Later on, we were discussing things such as who was to go, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said that there was no meeting that evening because you were busy with other talks, making decisions you mentioned, was it also discussed at that meeting who was to attend those talks and whether it was approved by the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please go back to the document first. I just noticed the date, July 13. On that day, we did have a meeting with your side. On that day, there was a meeting with you at check-point number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. To clarify that, let's scroll up so as to see the top of the document. Go further down the page in the Serbian. Further down. It says: "Delivered at 9.50." It means that this was done by the person typing it. So it wasn't up to me to put the date on the document.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to reiterate that there was a meeting on the 13th. On the 12th of July, in the evening, we had held the lengthy War Presidency meeting. There was another meeting on the 13th, in the evening or later in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recall when, on the 12th, you received this invitation, through UNPROFOR, to attend a meeting?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the invitation was received by Colonel Avdo Palic. As far as I remember, it was in the afternoon, perhaps around 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon. I know that we gathered in the evening and spent most of the night between the 12th and the 13th at that War Presidency session. This is what I recall in particular, and I speak from memory, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at the document, the second paragraph. It reads: "We were notified, through UNPROFOR, that during the day they were busy informing the population about the conditions of moving out of Zepa, and that they were forced to undertake such activities because of the Sarajevo government decision which stated that they shouldn't move. They want to secure the support of most of the population for the decision that was already made." Do you remember having conveyed this information to our representatives at Boksanica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I cannot exclude the possibility that somebody, say a member of the War Presidency, did that. But, personally, I did not have any contact with Dudnjik at the time. As far as I know, Colonel Palic was in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could he have informed them of this?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot exclude that, but as far as I remember, Colonel Palic on that day was in touch with Colonel Dudnjik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at para 4 next. Actually, para 5, where it says they informed most of the population and soldiers that they will all be granted free passage or that they would be allowed to stay in Zepa if they surrendered their weapons and recognised Serb authorities. Is it possible that this, too, was conveyed by Avdo Palic, that he told this to -- told Dudnjik about this, and that he passed it on to us?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I speak from memory. All contact with Dudnjik that day was through Colonel Palic. The overall situation and the feel at the War Presidency session that day does not reflect this information, at least how it was put in your report; for example, the fact that by that time there had already been a decision in place to move the entire population of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at lines 16 and 17, as well as further down the page. It is the fifth paragraph: "We informed the Zepa leadership, through UNPROFOR, that the process of evacuation and weapons surrender has to start at 900 hours on 15 July 1995. We are expecting their contacts and the decision." During that day, did you receive any information to this effect conveyed to him by the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. Whoever was in touch with Dudnjik probably forwarded this information to our side, if you had originally sent it to Dudnjik. However, I cannot recall this particular information, though. I don't think it was discussed, as such, at the War Presidency session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us this: Did Avdo Palic attend this Presidency session that lasted all night, and what were his positions and what did he inform you of? Is it possible that he might have conveyed all this information?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Palic was present at the session, and I believe that he was the one who conveyed the demands of the Serb side. But I don't remember it being in this shape and form. A discussion ensued regarding what that would mean for us, and then again the issue arose of what to do with the able-bodied men, and we immediately received those demands, and there was discussion on whether we should negotiate or not. But Colonel Palic did attend that meeting, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, were you told, via UNPROFOR, that you would have the option to either stay in Zepa or leave Zepa and surrender -- on condition that you surrender the weapons to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember every detail, but I tend to think that there were no such demands, or at least not formulated in that way. Now, whether Colonel Palic received all the details and perhaps then presented them to us in a somewhat different form, I don't know, but I don't recall that on the night of the 12th, going on the 13th, there were explicit demands, as shown here. I don't remember any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you discuss the fifth paragraph, where it says that: "A number of wealthy Muslims inquire, through the UNPROFOR, about the possibility to move out to the territory of the FRY or third countries with their movable property. They wanted to avoid mobilisation in the so-called ABiH." Now, this was relayed to us via UNPROFOR. Now, whether he had actually said this to UNPROFOR or not, can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember any of these details. As I've already said, I did not take part in these negotiations or these exchanges of messages, so I can't really say either way. But as far as I remember, it was not presented to the War Presidency at the meeting held on the night of the 12th and 13th of June [as interpreted], 1995, in this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to nip this one in the bud, I think we have our familiar month issue, if you look at the transcript. At least on mine, at page 75, line 24, there's a reference to the 12th and 13th of June, 1995. I think we've had this before. I just want to clarify that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tolimir has misspoken. It must be July. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It was July, indeed, and I thank Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question: Do you have any knowledge about whether part of the population really wanted to move out, via the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to third countries so they would avoid joining fighting; for instance, to the US or other places?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not rule out the possibility that there was talk to that effect and that some of the wealthy inhabitants of Zepa maybe voiced their positions in that respect. But I don't recall that as coming to the War Presidency as a specific request. If that was the case and if they did actually send such a request to someone, that is something that I cannot rule out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber about the way that the discussion proceeded on the meeting that night on the 12th, going on the 13th of July? How did that evolve; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember the following: I think Colonel Palic briefed us and said that he had received from Colonel Dudnjik, the UNPROFOR commander in Zepa, a request of the Serb side for negotiations. That was the major -- that was the gist of what Colonel Palic conveyed to us. Now, whether he also mentioned some of the details that you showed us in this report, I can't really recall. But as I've already said before, he did not convey most of these details to the War Presidency. Our overall concern at this meeting was -- or, actually, focused on two major areas. The first one was whether we were authorised and competent to actually negotiate, to enter these negotiations, and in that sense we submitted that request to the civilian and military authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, asking for their opinion on whether we had the authority to negotiate at the local level. That was the first area. The second area that was in our focus was probably conjectures and guessing as to what kind of demands we would be presented from the Serb side, because that was the day when Srebrenica fell. We could only assume what those demands might entail. The entire discussion that whole night on the night of the 12th and 13th revolved around these two major issues. As for these details and the specific demands that the Serb side presented, I can't recall any of that. We also discussed at length the option where we would receive a negative response from Sarajevo or Tuzla, if they were to say that we were not allowed to negotiate at the local level. But then the position prevailed that we should try and see how best to deal with this, because in the end it was our fate and our skins that we had to consider. But whatever somebody on the side would have to say in the final analysis, their lives were not at stake because they were not in Zepa. So that was the prevailing tone of all the discussions at this session of the War Presidency in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to the meeting of 13th July 1995. In examination-in-chief, when asked by the Prosecutor when you left from Zepa to Boksanica, which was check-point 2 of UNPROFOR, you said you couldn't remember because it was a long time ago and that you didn't take any notes at the time. This was on page 4293, lines 6 and 7 on the transcript. My question is this: At the meeting in Boksanica, did you take any notes, did you write anything down, or was it the same as what you said of the 12th of July, that you did not take any notes?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the meeting of the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm referring to. And is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't remember whether I took any notes or not on that day, the 13th. And if I did, they would have been lost. So everything I said about that meeting and everything that is in my statement is really -- are things that I can just recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, since you can't recall this, I will remind you of what you said during the examination-in-chief. And if some of it is not correct, just say so. You said the following, and I quote: "As far as I can recall at this meeting, the Serb side was represented by Colonel Zdravko Tolimir, UNPROFOR was represented by Colonel Sejmon Dudnjik, and I was there, and Mujo Imamovic. At the very beginning of the meeting, General Tolimir said something to the effect of this, Srebrenica has fallen, now it is Zepa's turn. We have two options here. We are offering the following: You should all -- you can all leave Zepa, be evacuated, board buses, and leave. And then I asked him whether that meant that people who were 35 years old could join their families and move out to the territories of the BH Army, and General Tolimir said, Yes, of course. And then if we decided to refuse the first option, the second option would be -- or the second alternative would be the military option; in other words, the military occupation of Zepa." And then you said the meeting did not last long and so on. I believe that my translators translated this properly and conveyed your words correctly. This is on transcript page 4294, lines 8 through 21. I tried to quote what you said.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's exactly what I said. They translated that properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, here we are talking of events 15 years ago. This event is significant for me and for you; for me, because I'm the accused in these proceedings, and for you, because you had to make decisions about the Srebrenica civilian population. Now, my question is this: Before you came to testify here, did you check and go through any of the documents relating to the meeting of the 13th of July or is everything that you have said here actually reconstruction based on your recollection?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything I said here was based on what I could remember. I had no notes of any kind, and I didn't read up on this subject before I came to testify here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: At this meeting, as well as the ones that followed with General Mladic, was the key issue, in fact, the surrender of weapons of the BH Army in Zepa and the surrender of the weapons that the able-bodied men had? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the talks always involved a whole package deal, if I can put it that way. So it was they involved the evacuation of the civilians and the surrender of weapons and able-bodied men. At times, they would have to surrender these to the UNPROFOR, at other times to the VRS. But, in any case, it was always a package deal, if I can define it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please pull up 1D261. That is a document that is, in fact, part of the diary of Mr. Fortin. The Defence recently established, comparing this document with the diary, that the pagination is different, and in the electronic disclosure suite, the name of this colonel was not mentioned by Ms. Carolyn Edgerton. And could we have D585, page 60 in English. And I hope, when discussing this excerpt, that it does not fall under Rule 70 and that we may show it in public. On the 65 ter list disclosed to the Defence on the 5th of September in 2008, this document appears under number 751. And the Defence also referred to this document in its pre-trial brief which, again, is a public document. Could we please have page 2 in both the B/C/S and English versions. We would like to see paragraph 8, which reads as follows -- well, first of all, let the witness read through this document, and then I will read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have some problems with the numbers. You were mentioning 1D268, and then later on D589, but there is no document with the number D589. We have just reached D100. Can you help us? Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I may be able to offer a more direct solution. If I understand what General Tolimir wants to show the Trial Chamber, it is a report of a meeting that was held by Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic on the 13th of July, in the afternoon, and I believe what he is showing us here is a summary of that meeting that's contained in Colonel Fortin's diary. And as I think the Trial Chamber has already seen through Colonel Fortin's testimony, what he did was, basically, cut and paste some of the reports that he participated in into his diary, in addition to providing his own contemporaneous recollection. We actually have a copy of the actual report that this excerpt from the diary is reproducing, except without the actual formatting of the report. That report is already in evidence as P596, so we can go directly to P596 without having to go through the circuitous route of putting up Colonel Fortin's summary of it or reproduction of it. So if it's all the same to the Defence, we can look at the real McCoy, as it were, P596, and look at the actual report, itself. And that did come in through Colonel Fortin, himself, originally, this report. So I just offer that instead of having to deal with all the translation issues that we had for Colonel Fortin's diary; for example, it's in French, it's in B/C/S, it's in English. There were three different versions of it that we need to juggle, and we can just go directly to 596.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, what do you think of this proposal of Mr. Thayer's? Is that helpful for your examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank Mr. Thayer. We wanted to see 1D261. It's all there. This should save me some time and enable me to put a few more questions. I have no idea what is in the documents offered by the Prosecution. Let's look at page 2 in Serbian, and it will all be crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we have the same document on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do. Paragraph 8, which reads --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The CO of the Rogatica Brigade, accompanied by General Tolimir and local Bosnian authorities, met at Ukrainian check-point 2 at noon today. The Serbs asked the Bosnians in the Zepa pocket to drop their weapons, after which the civilian population may either leave or stay. The Bosnian authorities were due to meet immediately after in the village to discuss their options. The Serbs gave them until 3.30 p.m. to decide. At 6.30 p.m., an answer was still awaited. The Bosnians indicated they needed until noon tomorrow." That's all I wanted to quote from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a report of the Ukrainian Battalion commander sent to General Gobillard in Sarajevo. That was in the period of time when you were there. He mentions the choice given to civilians to leave or stay. If I recollect correctly, he based this on a document. Am I right in assuming this?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you want me to answer, exactly, the choice between leaving or staying, or what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The question is this: In this Ukrainian Battalion commander's report, does it not read that the civilians would be either allowed to either leave or stay? Does it say so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's in there in paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since Dudnjik kept notes, did he accurately inform his command, and would you allow for the possibility that this report is more accurate than yours or my recollection?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he kept notes, then that's it, although I don't know what exactly he wrote down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if there is evidence that Colonel Dudnjik kept notes, we'd appreciate knowing what that is. That's, I think, the first we've heard of Colonel Dudnjik allegedly having notes. If there is a basis for that statement in the record, we'd like to know what the basis is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We've heard that the Prosecution wants to raise a procedural matter before we adjourn today. Perhaps we can leave it at this point for today and continue with this document and the matter mentioned in this document for tomorrow. Is that possible? Then you could think about which part or which kind of document you would use for continuation of your examination. We have only three minutes left for today. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to put the last question for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Dudnjik participate in that conversation on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see him taking any notes?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly cannot remember. However, he was there and he did comment on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did he send this report to his command, the report I just read out?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If there is a document in existence to that effect, if it's an official document, then there you go, but I don't know what he sent to his superiors. On the right-hand side in the English version, I see that it's supposed to be a report, but I can't know what he wrote. Yes, he was at a meeting. Yes, he participated. But as for whether he kept notes, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My last question: Did he report from the meeting that I offered that civilians may either leave or go following the surrender of weapons? Did he report this to his command in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it's in the report, he did. I have no documents to rely on any of this. I cannot confirm this or deny. If it's in the report, I have no doubt that he wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this was merely an offer of his? Actually, he's discussing my offer, where I said that they could either leave or stay. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't keep notes, I don't remember that, but I cannot deny that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will stop now and resume tomorrow. Tomorrow, we'll have time enough to discuss all of UNPROFOR's reports, discussing these matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. This last question was, in fact, an interesting set of questions. That concludes your examination for today. We have to continue tomorrow. Will you address the Chamber with your procedure matter in the presence of the witness or --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the witness could be excused. There is no reason for him to be subjected to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, again, thank you very much for today's attendance, and we will continue tomorrow in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The three matters are: First, with respect to the Prosecution's ongoing compliance with the Trial Chamber's 92 bis decision generating the proper lists, delineating which categories the various exhibits fall into, the Trial Chamber granted us an additional 30 days on top of the 30 days the Trial Chamber had originally ordered. We have been working to comply. I can tell the Trial Chamber it is taking a lot longer than we even thought when we first asked for the additional 30 days. The process is extremely time-consuming to be able to identify the documents and then go through the entire transcripts to make sure that we've caught all of the exhibits and categorised them correctly. We will have a troche ready to go to Registry by this Friday. However, it will fall far short of the approximately 120 92 bis witnesses that were subject to the Trial Chamber's decision, about half of which were 92 bis straight and the other half of the 92 bis with cross. I can just tell the Trial Chamber that there's just no way that we're going to be able to finish this project in the near future, much less by this Friday. I can tell the Court it's going to require weekend time, which is not a problem because we're always working on the weekend anyway, but we're working on the weekend to get ready for our witnesses. So we're going to do what we can. What I propose is that we, every week, provide the Trial Chamber and Registry with a minimum of five packages -- five witnesses ready to go to the Registry so the Registry can make sure all the proper P numbers are assigned. The first troche that we'll have this Friday, I think, will number approximately a dozen witnesses. Doing the math, that's going to be another probably four months, at a rate of a minimum of five a week, before we can complete that project: I think we'll be able to do more than five a week, frankly, but some of these witnesses are extremely extensive, days and days of testimony, which is time-consuming, and unfortunately we do not have unlimited resources to do that. It's work that needs to be done, ultimately, with attorneys who have handled these witnesses overseeing and actually involved in the process, in addition to Ms. Stewart and some other members of the staff. So I would ask the Trial Chamber for the flexibility to allow us to proceed along that schedule, a minimum of five a week. I'm sure we can do better than five, but I'd hate to promise something and not be able to deliver, particularly how it's looking so far. So I spring that on the Trial Chamber, but I wanted to give the Trial Chamber a heads-up relatively in advance of this Friday's dead-line. That's item 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you: You mentioned, more or less, 12, a dozen, witnesses. Are they covered by the list of witnesses calling for September?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. What we have done is we have tried to at least prioritise the witnesses who are coming who are 92 bis with cross. There are a couple who are listed for September, some of the experts, for example, who are among that dozen. So, certainly, we've tried to prioritise those witnesses. And I should have added, the straight 92 bis witnesses, naturally, I think, would be towards the tail end, because we want to focus on the witnesses that are coming before the Trial Chamber, and that's how we've approached the project thus far, so that's where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that is appreciated, and the Chamber will consider your submission, and we'll come back to that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if I could go into private session very briefly for the other two matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to adjourn for the day. We will resume -- Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a brief administrative matter, Your Honours. This accused, that is, me, has been, for over 1.145 days, working here, and this affects my ability to actually work properly, and I would really appreciate it if you could see to it that the Detention Unit authorities no longer apply those measures.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat what exactly it was that was being done in the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were, I think, referring to the nightly checks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to the fact that in 24 hours, I am being checked on a number of occasions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, we are running out of time. And we have discussed that earlier, and you know our decision of last week. We will proceed with that problem, and you know our decision. We have to adjourn now. We can't go further. And we will resume tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15 in Courtroom I.
